content: The cost-effectiveness of different antibiotic classes for preventing infections during cesarean sections is uncertain. There is no clear evidence favoring one particular class of antibiotics over another. Narrow-spectrum antibiotics, such as cefazolin and metronidazole, are recommended as first-line options due to their low risk of resistance selection and adverse effects. Second-line options include amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, gentamicin, and cefuroxime. The availability of antibiotics significantly impacts equitable access, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. A study of 13,561 healthcare facilities in such regions found that fewer than 50% stocked 17 priority antibiotics. For example, third-generation intravenous cephalosporins like ceftriaxone and cefotaxime were available in only 50% and 8% of facilities, respectively. However, higher-level facilities offering cesarean sections may have better availability. There is no direct evidence on the impact of different antibiotic classes on health equity in cesarean section prophylaxis. Factors influencing antibiotic use by providers include concerns about infection risk, unnecessary antibiotic use, side effects, medicalization of birth, and antimicrobial resistance. Some providers are motivated by fear of postpartum infections and associated medico-legal risks. Antibiotic prescribing practices are influenced by written guidelines, professional norms, personal experience, and cost-effectiveness considerations. A systematic review on the perspectives of women and providers regarding antibiotic prophylaxis at birth identified mixed views. Some providers felt infection risk varied by environment, while others weighed the benefits of infection prevention against potential side effects. There is no evidence on women’s perspectives regarding the acceptability or feasibility of this intervention. The feasibility of implementing antibiotic prophylaxis at cesarean sections is generally supported, though factors such as local guidelines, professional norms, and antibiotic affordability may influence its practicality. Cost-effectiveness and equity impacts remain uncertain. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that minimally anti-staphylococcal cephalosporins (third-generation) may increase endometritis rates compared to non-anti-staphylococcal penicillins. There is insufficient evidence on neonatal outcomes, maternal side effects, well-being, satisfaction, and antimicrobial resistance. Various antibiotic regimens are likely acceptable and feasible for use during cesarean sections, but their cost-effectiveness and equity impacts are unclear.
